items_missed: The move date was never confirmed. Bri recapped the email, the origin address, the square footage and the destination, then jumped to 'it looks like we have an arrival time between 12:30 and 230' — but at no point in six and a half minutes did she or the customer say what day the move is. On an outbound call whose entire purpose is confirming an online booking, the date is the one field that most needs to be read back.

No agenda statement and no 'sound good?'. She went from 'How are you doing today?' straight to 'I was just calling in regards to your online booking' and then into data collection. The customer never knew how long this would take or that pricing was coming.

Additional rooms never asked — no garage, no storage unit, no patio or balcony question. On a house-to-apartment move where the customer is actively dividing her belongings between three destinations, the garage is exactly where the forgotten items live.

Special considerations never probed. The question asked was 'do we have anything that's in particular special to concerns fragile heavy' — that is an inventory question about items, not the access question the rubric calls for. No long walks, no narrow hallways, no tight turns. The customer had to volunteer the walk herself: 'you just literally go across the parking lot which is the sidewalks right there.'

Storage stops never asked — and storage was the organizing fact of this entire call. The customer said plainly, 'This is what I'm gonna store in, in storage so they just can't move around like a truck does... just take that and put it in the warehouse, put it in storage.' Bri correctly scoped the job down to the apartment portion, but never asked whether Einstein was touching the storage leg, where that storage is, or whether a second stop is coming. That is a booking-scope risk sitting in plain sight.

Additional stops never asked, for the same reason — a move being split three ways between a container company, a son, and a new apartment is the highest-risk possible setup for a surprise second stop on move day.

Packing needs never asked. The customer volunteered 'Everything else I'm able to take in my vehicle, so there's not gonna be any boxes' — which closed the box question but not the packing-service question, and a packing upsell was never offered on a house being emptied by a customer moving alone.

The moving-stressor question was never asked. This customer is downsizing out of a sold house into a one-bedroom apartment while her son takes some of her things and the buyers' container company takes the rest — a genuinely stressful setup she described at length — and she was never asked what she was worried about.

Hourly rate not framed per mover per hour. 'we do charge the hourly rate which is the $192 for the two movers and 26 foot box truck' gives the team rate but never the $96-per-mover structure, and no day-of-week tier was offered — no mention that a weekday could be cheaper.

No Worries Damage Coverage never mentioned. 'insurance' appeared once inside the what's-included list and that was the entire coverage conversation. No $2,000, no repair/replace/reimburse, no 60c/lb baseline. On a move carrying two bookcases, a couch, a love seat and a chair belonging to someone downsizing out of a home, that is the differentiator most likely to matter.

On-Time Guarantee never mentioned — and the arrival window was the one concrete commitment Bri made on this call ('an arrival time between 12:30 and 230'). Stating a window and then not stating what happens if Einstein misses it leaves the strongest reassurance on the table at the exact moment it would have landed.

The no-hidden-fees pitch was a single sentence — 'We do not have any hidden fees of any type just so you know' — with no itemized list. No credit card fees, no transportation fee, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees. The line is a claim; the list is what makes it credible.

No sense-check anywhere. The pricing, inclusions, no-fees claim and the full clock explanation ran as one unbroken ~130-word block, and the customer's entire contribution across it was 'Okay, okay. Okay.' Not one 'does that make sense?'

No typical time range for the home size. She asserted 'about a four hour move' without ever telling the customer what a partial one-bedroom normally runs, so the customer has no way to judge whether four hours is generous, tight, or right.

No dollar total was ever given. The customer was told the rate ($192/hr) and the hours (about four) and left to multiply. She never heard '$768', never heard a range, and never heard what the 2.5-hour minimum would cost if the crew finished early. A customer who cannot state her own estimate cannot compare it to a competitor's.

Stairs and the fourth-floor walk-up were captured and then never priced. The customer said 'it's on the fourth floor at the very top. They do have an elevator. You know, if they need to use it' — and 'I don't know what your guys prefer.' Bri asked the right follow-up about reserving the elevator, got 'I have no idea but you know I'll see if I can,' and left it there. An unreservable elevator at a fourth-floor destination is the single largest swing factor on this move's hours and it was never named as one.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors — no school-bus reference for the parking-lot walk, nothing to make four hours feel concrete.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. This was one of the best possible setups for it: the customer is already self-transporting ('Everything else I'm able to take in my vehicle'), already consolidating, and already splitting the load. She had done the work herself and nobody named it, credited it, or extended it. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload,' no close.
No deposit required was never mentioned — a free, unambiguous reassurance on a call with a customer who is coordinating around a house sale she does not control.

No bolded-details framing on the confirmation email, and no 'reply with any corrections' verification ask. What she got was 'you can just respond to the email that I'm going to send you' — offered as a channel for future questions, not as a request to check the details. That matters more than usual here, because Bri herself said the customer's notes had not come through: 'we've been having some issues with our system with people putting notes, our customers notes and then not showing up. So this is actually great. Cause I can run this up the ladder because it did not come through.' She diagnosed a data-loss problem on this exact record and then did not ask the customer to verify the record.
No hours and no direct phone number at close — 'you can reach out to us directly' without saying how or when.

Customer's name used twice ('may I speak with Joan?' and 'Hi Joan, this is bri calling') — short of the 3+ standard, and never once during the pricing or clock explanation where it would have broken up the monologue.
top_strength: Bri's best moment is one most reps would have skipped entirely. The customer explained that her online submission was wrong — the 855 square feet was only part of the picture, because the buyers' container company is taking one portion and her son is taking another. Instead of forcing the record to match the form, Bri re-scoped the job live and said so out loud: 'Gotcha. Okay, understood so we will do this as a partial one bedroom move,' then confirmed it against the destination — 'Yeah, like a one bedroom apartment ish cause we'll have bedroom living area' — and the customer landed on it with her: 'Pretty much, yeah, exactly and yeah, and that's exactly what I'm moving into, it's gonna be a one bedroom.' That is the correct instinct on the highest-value estimate-accuracy behavior there is: the form said 855 square feet of a house, and the truth was a partial one-bedroom with zero boxes. She also caught a real systems failure and escalated it in the same breath: 'I'm actually really glad that you said that we've been having some issues with our system with people putting notes, our customers notes and then not showing up. So this is actually great. Cause I can run this up the ladder because it did not come through, but that's okay we would call you anyways to confirm.' She turned a data loss into a reason the customer should feel good about the confirmation call, and flagged it upstream. That is the argument for why this outbound call exists at all. On top of that, she asked the single sharpest access question anyone asked this week — 'And can you reserve the elevator, is that just public?' — which is exactly the question that separates a four-hour fourth-floor move from a six-hour one.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Bri does the discovery well and then hands the customer nothing she can hold. There is no date read back, no dollar total, no typical range, and no written-verification ask — on a call where Bri herself discovered that the customer's notes had already been lost by the system once. The close should have been: 'So to confirm, Joan — Saturday the 26th, arrival between 12:30 and 2:30, two movers and a 26-foot truck at $192 an hour, and we're estimating about four hours, so roughly $768. I'm sending that to you right now with all of it bolded at the top — the date, the addresses, the rate and the estimate. Read it over and reply with any corrections, because I want to make sure the partial-move scope we just worked out actually lands in the file this time.' That one paragraph fixes the date, the total, the bolded list and the verification ask, and it uses the systems problem she already surfaced as the reason the customer should check. Second priority: the fourth-floor elevator is the unresolved variable and it was left with the customer. 'I'll see if I can, I have no idea' is not a plan. Either Bri books the elevator question as a follow-up she owns, or she tells the customer what happens to the estimate if the elevator is not available — because a four-hour estimate with an elevator and a four-hour estimate with three flights of stairs are not the same move. Third, the differentiators: this call landed Meet Your Mover cleanly and nothing else. No Worries Damage Coverage and the On-Time Guarantee were both free points sitting right next to things Bri already said. She stated an arrival window and did not say what happens if we miss it; she said 'insurance' and did not say $2,000 or repair-replace-reimburse. Estimate-accuracy flag for the bottom-4 review: four hours for a partial one-bedroom with zero boxes and a one-story origin is on the high side and cannot be checked, because Bri never stated a typical range for the home size and never gave a dollar total. The padding here is not as blatant as quoting past a stated range — it is worse in one specific way, which is that there is no stated range to measure it against. Get the typical-range line back into the script ('a partial one-bedroom like this usually runs us two and a half to four hours'), then say where this job falls in it and why. Worth pulling the actual against this one when it runs, particularly to see what the fourth-floor elevator did to the hours. Finally, this call is 0/10 on Save Your Ass on a customer who was already doing it — she is taking every box in her own vehicle. 'Joan, you're already doing the thing that saves the most money here — everything you can carry yourself is time off our clock. Keep going with the small stuff, the loose items in drawers, anything off the walls, and by the time we show up it's just the furniture. Does that make sense?' That costs fifteen seconds, it validates what she is already doing, and it is the one behavior that actually moves the estimate.
phone_presence_notes: Genuinely warm and natural language throughout — 'I'm actually really glad that you said that,' 'Awesome,' 'You are so welcome. Have a good rest of your weekend' — and she let the customer tell the whole container-company story without cutting her off, which is what produced the correct re-scope; the score stops at 4 rather than 5 because the name was used only twice, the entire pricing-and-clock section ran as one unbroken block that reduced the customer to 'Okay, okay,' and no question ever acknowledged that downsizing out of a sold house might be stressful.
audio_review_reason: The clarity-and-pace bullet was deducted on transcript evidence that is ambiguous. The pricing block runs as one continuous stretch with several garbled passages — 'it looks like we've got you all med up the system,' 'all rap pads, advance protect items when being moved,' and a sentence that simply stops at 'the time is prorated in fifteen minute.' Audio is needed to tell whether she was genuinely running words together at speed or whether this is transcription artifact over a clear delivery, and to confirm whether the customer's string of 'Okay, okay' reads as tracking or as lost.
